lines: A large dbt project's full CI run rebuilds every single model, on every single pull request, no matter what actually changed.
Most of what gets rebuilt is work nobody touched at all -- the same output, computed again, for no real reason.
A single-model change, run through a state-aware build instead, builds only that one model and whatever actually sits downstream of it.
Same change, same guarantee of correctness, a measurably smaller amount of work actually done.
Worth predicting before the next few steps answer it directly.
A full rebuild is certainly safe -- it genuinely tests every single model in the project, with nothing left out.
Is testing absolutely everything the only way to be safe about one small, specific change?
Or is there a smaller set of models that's just as safe to test?
steps.answer: No, a full rebuild isn't the only safe option. Everything a change could possibly reach is exactly the changed model plus everything downstream of it -- nothing sitting outside that set could have been affected at all.

lines: Here's the first real mechanism, built specifically around that exact idea.
Compare the current project against a stored manifest from the last known-good build.
Select the node that changed, plus everything downstream of it, using that same comparison.
Everything else gets deferred straight to its already-built production relation instead of being rebuilt from scratch.
Here's a second, independent mechanism built around the same underlying idea.
A plan previews exactly what a change would affect, computing nothing until that preview is actually verified.
Once it's verified, promotion repoints production directly at what was already built and tested in development.
No recomputation happens at that point, and no data actually moves -- it's a pointer swap, not a rebuild.
steps.takeaway: A verified output does not need to be computed twice to be trusted in production.

lines: One more question worth sitting with before the reveal that follows it.
A model's overall shape, its name and its grain, can look exactly the same from the outside after a change.
Does an unchanged model-level contract mean nothing underneath it could possibly have broken?
Or can something real break while the surface of the contract stays exactly the same?
steps.answer: No, an unchanged contract doesn't mean nothing broke. A single column being renamed or having its type changed is still breaking, for any consumer reading that exact column, even while the model around it looks completely untouched.

lines: Here's that exact risk, caught directly, using the very column rename this chapter warned about earlier.
Jumping straight to a new column name, skipping the expand phase entirely, gets flagged as a breaking change immediately.
The identical underlying change, done properly through expand first -- adding the new column while keeping the old one -- is not flagged as breaking at all.
Same destination, two different paths there, and only one of those two paths earns a breaking-change warning.
Now a different kind of tradeoff, measured rather than simply assumed.
Testing the full table catches every single one of a known, fixed set of planted bugs, with nothing missed.
A small, fixed, seeded sample runs much faster, but checked against that exact same set of planted bugs, it only catches whichever fraction happened to land inside it.
That's a real, measured tradeoff between CI speed and actual bug coverage, not a hypothetical one.
steps.takeaway: A seeded sample only ever catches the bugs that happen to land inside it.

lines: A build can fail for reasons that have nothing to do with a wrong value at all.
An expected dependency between two models can silently disappear, breaking the lineage a downstream model was actually relying on.
Separately, a measured latency can cross this chapter's own SLO threshold before the change carrying it ever reaches production.
Both of those get checked and failed right here in CI, before the merge happens, not discovered afterward in production.
Pulling every piece of this topic together into one shape.
Two genuinely different mechanisms, state:modified plus defer and a virtual environment's promotion, both build only what a change could actually reach.
A column-level check catches a contract that looks unchanged but genuinely isn't, and a seeded sample's coverage tradeoff gets measured instead of assumed.
And a CI gate can now fail on a broken lineage edge or a breached SLO, not only on a wrong computed value.
steps.takeaway: A fast CI run and a safe CI run are the same thing once it builds exactly what a change could reach.

lines: One real comparison to close on, run for real rather than just described.
Take the shop's own model graph and change exactly one model inside it.
Run a full rebuild against that single change, and separately run state:modified plus defer against the identical change.
Does the state-aware build end up building roughly the same number of models as the full rebuild, or does it genuinely build fewer?
steps.answer: It genuinely builds fewer models. The state-aware build selects only the changed model and whatever sits downstream of it, correctly skipping every model the change could not possibly have reached.
